nodes.name: AI Problem Solving Foundations
nodes.description: Representing problems using states, actions, initial state, goal test, and path cost.
misconceptions: An AI problem is only a list of possible answers.

An AI problem is only a list of possible: A search problem is just a list of all the possible answers.

nodes.name: Graph Basics
nodes.description: Nodes, edges, directed graphs, paths, and graph traversal.
misconceptions: An edge always has the same cost.
A node and an edge represent the same thing.

All edges in a graph have equal cost.
Every edge costs the same amount.
A node and an edge represent the same th: Nodes and edges are the same thing.
A node is the same as an edge.

nodes.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
nodes.description: Explores the frontier level by level, typically using a FIFO queue.
misconceptions: BFS is always the lowest-cost algorithm.
BFS uses a stack.

BFS always finds the cheapest path in a weighted graph.
BFS gives the lowest cost path even when edge costs differ.
BFS expands nodes in last in first out order.
BFS works with a stack like DFS.

resources: Exercise: shortest path in an unweighted graph

nodes.name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
nodes.description: Explores a branch deeply before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.
misconceptions: DFS always finds the shortest path.
DFS cannot revisit or backtrack.

DFS always gives the shortest path.
DFS is guaranteed to find the optimal path.
DFS never goes back once it moves forward.

resources: Exercise: trace DFS with a visited set

nodes.name: Path Cost g(n)
nodes.description: Accumulated cost from the start node to the current node.
misconceptions: Path cost is the estimated remaining cost to the goal.
Only the most recent edge contributes to g(n).

Path cost is the estimated remaining cos: g(n) is the estimated cost from the node to the goal.
Path cost means the distance still left to reach the goal.
Only the most recent edge contributes to: g(n) is just the cost of the last edge.
Path cost only counts the final step, not the whole path.

resources: Exercise: compare two routes with edge weights

nodes.name: Queues and Priority Queues
nodes.description: Data structures for managing the frontier; priority queues remove the item with the best priority.
misconceptions: A priority queue always removes the earliest inserted item.
A priority queue and FIFO queue are interchangeable.

A priority queue always removes the earl: A priority queue pops the first item that was added.
A priority queue works first in first out.
A priority queue and FIFO queue are inte: A priority queue is the same as a normal FIFO queue.
You can use a regular queue instead of a priority queue.

resources: Exercise: update and pop frontier entries

nodes.name: Heuristic h(n)
nodes.description: An estimate of the remaining cost from a node to the goal.
misconceptions: h(n) is the cost already paid.
A heuristic must always equal the true remaining cost.

h(n) is the cost so far from the start.
The heuristic is the cost already spent to reach the node.
A heuristic must always equal the true r: The heuristic has to be the exact cost to the goal.
A heuristic is only valid if it equals the real remaining cost.

nodes.name: Uniform-Cost Search (UCS)
nodes.description: Expands the frontier node with the lowest accumulated path cost g(n).
misconceptions: UCS prioritizes the smallest heuristic value.
UCS is equivalent to BFS even with unequal edge costs.

UCS prioritizes the smallest heuristic v: Uniform cost search picks the node with the lowest h(n).
UCS uses the heuristic to choose which node to expand.
UCS is equivalent to BFS even with unequ: UCS and BFS behave the same with different edge costs.
Uniform cost search is just BFS.

nodes.name: Greedy Best-First Search
nodes.description: Chooses the frontier node with the lowest heuristic h(n).
misconceptions: Greedy search always finds an optimal path.
Greedy prioritizes g(n)+h(n).

Greedy search always finds an optimal pa: Greedy best-first search is guaranteed to give the shortest path.
Greedy best-first search orders nodes by f(n) = g(n) + h(n).
Greedy search uses both path cost and the heuristic.

nodes.name: A* Search
nodes.description: Prioritizes nodes using f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining path cost so far and estimated remaining cost.
misconceptions: A* uses only h(n).
A* uses only g(n).
A* is guaranteed optimal for every heuristic and every implementation.

A* only looks at the heuristic and ignores path cost.
A* picks the node with the smallest h(n) only.
A* only uses path cost and ignores the heuristic.
A* orders the frontier by g(n) alone.
A* is guaranteed optimal for every heuri: A* is always optimal with any heuristic.
A* always returns the shortest path no matter what heuristic I use.

resources: Exercise: calculate g, h, and f for each frontier node

nodes.name: Admissible and Consistent Heuristics
nodes.description: A heuristic is admissible if it never overestimates the true remaining cost. A* with an admissible heuristic returns an optimal path.
misconceptions: An overestimating heuristic still guarantees an optimal A* path.
Any heuristic that gives a plausible-looking estimate is admissible.

An overestimating heuristic still guaran: A heuristic that overestimates still gives an optimal A* path.
Overestimating is fine, A* will still find the best path.
Any heuristic that gives a plausible-loo: Any reasonable looking estimate counts as an admissible heuristic.
A heuristic is admissible as long as it looks like a sensible guess.
